itemTypes.meal: Lunch or dinner, including working sessions over food

items.title: Registration, badge collection and coffee
Welcome remarks and introductory presentations
items.subtitle: From COP31 commitments to investment-ready planning
items.summary: Welcome remarks from IRENA, GIZ, Germany's Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) and Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWE), Denmark and the Clean Energy Ministerial (CEM), followed by introductions to the LTES Network and to GET.transform.

items.title: Keynote presentation
Electrification and the outcomes of COP31 – what scenarios must now capture
items.summary: This opening session examines what accelerated electrification commitments mean for national energy planning. Government planners and the institutions supporting them discuss how global electrification goals translate into national scenarios, policies and investment pipelines, and what practical support countries need to make that translation work.

items.title: Coffee break
Building planning ecosystems that survive political cycles
items.partner: Co-hosted with the Energy Modelling Hub and Natural Resources Canada
items.summary: Durable scenario work depends on institutions. This session examines how countries build planning ecosystems that develop and retain capacity across ministries, universities and research institutions, moving from dependence on external support toward self-sustaining national planning functions. It covers institutional mandates and ownership, skills and retention, modelling-tool institutionalisation, and alignment with policy and budget cycles.

items.title: Lunch break
Data governance, sharing and quality assurance for developing long-term scenarios
items.partner: Co-hosted with European Commission DG ENER
items.summary: Credible scenarios rest on credible data, yet many planning teams face fragmented access, persistent gaps and heavy reliance on proprietary datasets. This session examines how countries and regional institutions govern, share and quality-assure energy data – from national energy information systems to regional databases – and explores practical solutions for planning teams with limited resources.

items.title: Welcome dinner

days.label: Day 2
days.theme: Scenarios for Security, Flexibility and Implementation

items.title: Coffee and networking
Closed-door session: LTES Network members and partners strategic meeting
items.access: Closed-door: LTES Network members and partners only
items.note: Coffee and networking continue for other participants until 09:15.

items.title: Impact session: Brazil's national energy plan and the LTES Network
items.summary: Brazil's Energy Research Office presents the country's national energy planning instruments, the long-term PNE 2055 and the ten-year expansion plan PDE 2035, and reflects on how peer exchange through the LTES Network informed national planning practice. An impact spotlight on what Network collaboration looks like for national planning processes.

items.title: Coffee break
Planning under geopolitical uncertainty
items.partner: Co-hosted with the World Energy Council
items.summary: Geopolitical volatility, fuel-price shocks and supply disruptions have moved energy security back to the centre of national planning. This session examines how countries stress-test scenarios against these risks, how the fossil-fuel transition and stranded-asset exposure are treated in national frameworks, and how alternative plans are conceived to respond to supply disruptions.

items.title: Lunch session: state-of-the-art showcase of machine learning and artificial intelligence in energy planning
items.summary: A working-lunch showcase of applied AI uses prioritised by the LTES Network – demand and load forecasting, scenario development and sensitivity analysis, and data processing and quality assurance.

items.title: Climate risks and adaptation in national energy scenarios
items.summary: Climate variability and physical risks – heatwaves, floods, droughts and shifting hydrology – are stress-testing national energy systems in real time. This session examines how planning teams incorporate climate risks and adaptation into long-term scenarios: from El Niño-driven droughts in hydropower-dependent systems to cooling demand and flood exposure, and the data and methods needed to make plans resilient.

items.title: Coffee break
Transformative scenarios in national planning practice
items.summary: Scenario practice is evolving: deep uncertainty and robust decision-making, agent-based and participatory modelling, and open-source tools are moving from research into government planning, bringing new actors and interdisciplinary insights into the scenario-building process itself. This session examines how these methods can be navigated within the realities government planners face: resource constraints, institutional mandates and political viability.

items.title: Day 2 wrap and bridge to Day 3
items.summary: Joint reflections by IRENA and GET.transform.

days.label: Day 3
days.theme: From Planning to Investment and Implementation
days.intro: Convened under the Global Coalition for Energy Planning (GCEP), the Planning–Investment Dialogue connects the technical discussions of the LTES Forum with the investment and implementation challenges emerging from GCEP regional dialogues. The morning takes the findings of those dialogues as its evidence base and opens a structured discussion with financiers, regulators and planning institutions on a single question: what turns an energy plan into an investable opportunity. It focuses on the practical interface between planning and investment: what countries are asking from their planning systems; which bottlenecks recur across regions – grids, flexibility, project preparation, institutional coordination, finance-facing signals – and what support partners are prepared to offer in response.

items.title: Coffee and networking
Opening: from the LTES Forum to investment-ready implementation
Scene-setting presentation: findings from the GCEP regional planning-to-investment dialogues
items.subtitle: What countries are telling us about planning, investment and implementation
items.summary: Cross-regional findings from the GCEP regional dialogues and other relevant regional exchanges, focusing on recurring planning-to-investment messages: grids and flexibility, institutional coordination, project preparation, finance-facing planning signals, data and governance, and country requests for practical partner support.

items.title: From energy planning to investment decisions
items.summary: This session examines how developing countries can strengthen the connection between national energy planning and investment decisions. Drawing on country experiences and perspectives from development finance institutions, it explores how long-term scenarios inform investment priorities, how these priorities connect with budgeting and project preparation, and how collaboration between planners and financiers can support implementation.

items.title: Coffee break
Planning the transition away from fossil fuels
items.partner: Co-hosted with the Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge, Spain
items.summary: The transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) agenda through the lens of investment-ready energy planning: how national planning systems can translate transition-away commitments into credible implementation pathways, and what practical support GCEP can provide to facilitate dialogue between planners, policymakers and financiers on the conditions needed to move from political commitment to investable action. It also reflects on the development and climate nexus.

items.title: Lunch break and interactive lunch session on energy access planning
items.summary: Lunch from 13:00. The interactive session on energy access planning runs from 13:15 to 14:15; a description will follow.

items.title: From plans to delivery – how can planning support enabling energy markets?
items.summary: What it takes to turn energy planning priorities into commercially viable projects, infrastructure and functioning markets. The session looks at what needs to happen from planning to action, from policy, regulation and procurement to market design and investment decisions, and where key barriers can emerge along the way, bringing together perspectives from different actors on how governments and planning institutions can create the conditions for investment and strengthen the link between long-term planning and delivery.

items.title: Coffee break
Country cases – when planning meets the market
items.summary: Country case presentations from three angles. Planning enables the market (large scale): how long-term planning can inform large-scale project procurement and create a pipeline investors can respond to. The market moves faster than planning (distributed generation): what happens when markets, prosumers or new technologies such as battery storage move ahead of the assumptions in the plan, and how market information, investor behaviour, technology costs and emerging business models should feed back into planning. Planning enables infrastructure investment: how grid infrastructure enables functioning energy markets and private investment, and how planning can provide the long-term visibility, coordination and investment framework needed to develop it.

items.title: Closing of Day 3
Breakfast session: Connecting long-term energy scenarios with marine spatial planning
items.subtitle: How closer coordination can lead to better results
items.summary: Marine spatial planning (MSP) is the strategic process through which governments decide how marine space is used over time, balancing ecological, social and economic objectives across sectors. It is a key enabler of accelerated, responsible offshore wind deployment, and well-planned processes can shorten lead times and reduce development costs. Long-term energy scenarios, in turn, explore future energy mixes and infrastructure needs, in which offshore wind plays a growing role for countries with strong resources. This session examines how energy planners and marine spatial planners can work together so that each process informs the other – connecting scenarios with more granular MSP data on available areas to improve forecasts of timelines and of transmission, interconnection and supporting infrastructure needs. Building on discussions throughout the Week, it focuses on institutional coordination and data governance.

items.title: Greening data centres: principles for sound energy planning under uncertainty
items.summary: The rapid expansion of data centres is creating new challenges for energy planners, particularly in anticipating electricity demand, assessing grid capacity and planning future infrastructure investments. This session explores how integrated planning approaches can help governments accommodate growing data centre demand while considering system reliability, flexibility, affordability and broader energy priorities.

items.title: Planning for power system flexibility – from scenarios to grid investment
items.partner: Co-hosted with the Green Grids Initiative
items.summary: How governments can integrate flexibility needs into long-term energy planning as renewable energy shares increase and power systems evolve. Drawing on country experiences and technical perspectives, the discussion examines the implications for grid expansion, storage, system operation and investment priorities, including the planning and coordination approaches needed to support more flexible and resilient power systems.

items.title: Coffee break
Regional energy planning – aligning national priorities and regional interconnection
items.partner: Co-hosted with the African Union Commission
items.summary: Regional institutions and planning entities from different world regions share how national plans inform regional transmission development and vice versa, the institutional mechanisms that support coordination, and the challenges that remain.
